challenges.name: audit-log-quiz
challenges.title: What does the audit log prove?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the support agent's audit trail: a wrapper that writes its record after the tool returns, and a hash chain that still verifies after the newest record was deleted.

questions.explanation: True. The append runs only after await tools[name](args) returns. refund_order threw while reading the provider's response, after the refund had already been issued, so the exception skipped the append and left the function: the money moved, and the audit log has nothing. Writing the record in a finally block (or catching, recording outcome "error" and rethrowing) records every call, and failed calls are often the ones an investigation needs most. The misconception is that a failed tool call did nothing worth recording.

questions.question:
Audit records of session s_5 (hashes shortened). Each hash is sha256(prevHash + "\n" + canonicalJson(record without prevHash and hash)); GENESIS is 64 zeros.

#1 staff_09 lookup_order ok      prev=000000000000 hash=3f9a1c07d2e8
#2 u_2207   refund_order denied  prev=3f9a1c07d2e8 hash=b82e55a0c914
#3 staff_09 refund_order ok      prev=b82e55a0c914 hash=0c7d3e9f61ab

Someone with write access to the audit table deleted record #3. The nightly job runs verifyChain over the table:

verify: ok

Statement: "Because verifyChain still returns ok, no record has been removed from this log."
questions.explanation: False. A hash chain links each record to the one before it, so removing or editing a record in the middle breaks the next record's prevHash and verification fails there. Removing the newest record leaves a shorter chain that is still internally consistent: nothing after #2 points at the deleted #3. To detect that, the latest hash (the head) has to be stored somewhere the writer cannot change - for example published every few minutes to a separate write-once store - and verification compares the table's last hash and count with it. The misconception is that a valid chain proves the log is complete; it proves only that the records you have were not changed in place.

challenges.name: audited-tool-executor
challenges.title: Audit every tool call, with a hash chain
challenges.description:
Compliance asked who refunded order ord_8812 and could not get an answer: the support agent's tool calls were logged only when they succeeded, with full arguments (an access token included), and anyone with access to the log table could edit a line. Write AuditedExecutor, the wrapper every tool call of the CodeDev support agent goes through.

execute(ctx, tool, args) - ctx { sessionId, userId } comes from the host's authenticated session, never from the model:
1. start = clock.now(). Look the tool up as an own property of tools only (the model can ask for a tool named "toString").
2. Unknown tool: outcome "error", message "unknown tool: <tool>", nothing runs. Otherwise, policy(ctx.userId, tool) false: outcome "denied", the tool does NOT run. Otherwise run tools[tool](args): a return value gives "ok" (return it unchanged as value); a throw gives "error" with the thrown Error's message, or String(thrown) if it is not an Error.
3. Append exactly one record (also when the tool threw), then return { outcome: "ok", value } | { outcome: "error", message } | { outcome: "denied" }. Tools may advance the fake clock; durationMs = clock.now() after the call - start.

Record: seq (1, 2, ...), at = new Date(start).toISOString(), sessionId, userId, tool (the requested name), args = summarizeArgs(args) (for denied and unknown calls too), outcome, error (the message cut with the 64-character rule below, null unless outcome is "error"), durationMs, prevHash (the previous record's hash; GENESIS = 64 zeros for the first), hash = sha256 hex (node:crypto) of prevHash + "\n" + canonicalJson(the record without prevHash and hash).

canonicalJson(value): JSON with no spaces, object keys sorted at every depth with the default sort(), array order kept; undefined (a call without args) is written as null.

summarizeArgs(args), in this order: (a) at any depth, inside arrays too, a key whose name lowercased with "_" and "-" removed contains password, token, secret, apikey or authorization gets the value "[REDACTED]", whatever it was; (b) every other string value longer than 64 characters becomes its first 64 characters + "...(+N chars)" (N = characters removed); (c) canonicalJson of the result; (d) if that is longer than 200 characters: its first 200 characters + "...(truncated)". Lengths are JavaScript string lengths.

verifyChain(records): in array order, record i must have prevHash = GENESIS (i = 0) or records[i - 1].hash, else reason "prev_hash"; and hash = the hash recomputed from its own fields, else reason "hash". Return { ok: true } or { ok: false, brokenAt: <seq of the first broken record>, reason }.

Input (one JSON test case on stdin, read by the runner): the fake tools, the allow-list used as policy, the calls in time order and optional tamper scenarios applied to copies of your records. Output: one line per call with your record (hashes shortened to 12 characters) and the value you returned, the number of tool runs, verifyChain on your records and on each tampered copy. With "summary": true only totals and the last hash are printed. Keep the types and the test runner unchanged.
hints: If a tool throws halfway through, which line of your execute() still runs? Every path - unknown tool, denied, ok, thrown - has to reach the same "append a record" step exactly once.

Write three small helpers before execute: canonicalJson (recursive, sort the keys of plain objects, leave arrays in order), a recursive clean step for summarizeArgs (check each key before looking at its value), and one function that hashes a record from its prevHash and its other fields. Use that same hash function in execute and in verifyChain, so the two can never disagree.

A similar chain on different data: three log lines A, B, C with h0 = 64 zeros, hA = sha256(h0 + "
" + json(A)), hB = sha256(hA + "
" + json(B)), hC = sha256(hB + "
" + json(C)). Edit B and keep hB: recomputing B's hash fails at B. Recompute hB too: B looks fine but C.prevHash no longer equals B's hash, so the check fails at C. Delete C: nothing points at it, so only a copy of the last hash kept elsewhere can tell.
